options: Nothing: ill-formed, a requires-expression needs a parameter list
Nothing: ill-formed, `sizeof(T) > 4` is not a requirement
questions.explanation: `sizeof(T) > 4;` is a simple requirement, which only checks that the expression is valid. For `char` it is valid and evaluates to `false`, but the value is never looked at, so `Big<char>` is `true`. To test the value, write a nested requirement `requires sizeof(T) > 4;` inside the braces, or define the concept as `sizeof(T) > 4` directly. The parameter list of a requires-expression is optional.

options: Well-formed: `f` accepts types larger than four bytes
Well-formed, but the constraint is always satisfied
Ill-formed: a constraint must be a concept-id
Ill-formed: `sizeof(T) > 4` must be parenthesized in a requires-clause
questions.explanation: The operands of a requires-clause must be primary expressions joined by `&&` or `||`. `sizeof(T)` is not a primary expression, so it cannot be the clause's operand and the declaration is ill-formed. Writing `requires (sizeof(T) > 4)` makes the whole comparison a parenthesized primary expression. Constraints are not limited to concept-ids; any constant `bool` expression works once it is parenthesized.

options: `signed_integral` then `integral`
Nothing: the call `f(1)` is ambiguous
`integral` then `integral`
`signed_integral` then nothing: `f(1u)` is ill-formed
questions.explanation: For `f(1)` both templates are viable with identical parameter types, so the more constrained one wins. `std::signed_integral<T>` is defined as `std::integral<T> && std::is_signed_v<T>`, which normalizes to a conjunction containing the very same atom as `std::integral`, so it subsumes it. For `f(1u)` only the first template is satisfied. Ambiguity would arise only if the two concepts were written independently.

options: Well-formed: it calls the `Int32` overload, which has more requirements
Ill-formed: the call is ambiguous
Well-formed: it calls the `Integral` overload, which was declared first
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required
questions.explanation: Subsumption compares atomic constraints by identity, and two atoms are identical only if they come from the same expression in the source. The `std::is_integral_v<T>` in `Int32` is a different atom from the one in `Integral`, so neither constraint subsumes the other and the call is ambiguous. Defining `Int32` as `Integral<T> && sizeof(T) == 4` makes the `Int32` overload win.

options: Nothing: ill-formed, `t` cannot be used in a compound requirement
It depends on whether `P` is an aggregate
questions.explanation: A return-type requirement `-> C` checks `C<decltype((e))>`, with the doubled parentheses. `t.x` is an lvalue, so `decltype((t.x))` is `int&`, and `std::same_as<int&, int>` is false. Reading it as `decltype(t.x)`, which would be `int`, is what makes `1` tempting. Use `std::same_as<int&>` or `std::convertible_to<int>` instead.

questions.prompt: What happens when this program is compiled?
options: It compiles and `main` returns 0: `1` converts to `true`
It compiles and `main` returns 1: the constraint is not satisfied
Ill-formed: the call is ambiguous
Ill-formed: the atomic constraint `T::value` has type `int`, not `bool`
questions.explanation: Substitution into the atom `T::value` succeeds, so the result must be a constant expression of type exactly `bool`; no conversion is applied, and an `int` makes the program ill-formed rather than leaving the constraint unsatisfied. The "not satisfied" reading applies only when substitution itself fails, for example if `S` had no `value` at all. Writing `requires (T::value != 0)` or `requires bool(T::value)` fixes it.

questions.prompt: What does the C++23 standard say about this translation unit?
options: Both assertions pass, since `foo` is found by the time of the second
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required
The second assertion must fail, because concept results are cached
Ill-formed: `foo` must be declared before the concept
questions.explanation: The atomic constraint `requires(T t) { foo(t); }` with `T = S` is false at the first assertion and would be true at the second. [temp.constr.atomic] makes a program ill-formed, no diagnostic required, when identical atomic constraints with identical arguments have different satisfaction results at different points. GCC and Clang both remember the first result and fail the second assertion, which is why the third option is tempting, but the standard does not require that.

questions.prompt: What does the C++23 standard say about this program?
options: Well-formed: `main` returns 1
Ill-formed: `Odd` does not satisfy `std::equality_comparable`
Undefined behavior
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required
questions.explanation: `Odd` satisfies the syntactic part of `std::equality_comparable`, so the call compiles, but it does not model the concept, whose semantic requirements make `==` an equivalence relation and `a == a` true. [res.on.requirements] says a program whose validity or meaning depends on a concept being modelled, when it is only satisfied, is ill-formed, no diagnostic required. Returning 1 is what you will probably observe, which is exactly why the rule is easy to miss.
